title: Banking Awareness
summary: The GA section of banking mains (IBPS PO/Clerk, SBI, RBI exams) asks a fixed block of banking questions: the RBI and its rates, bank types, banking terms, financial institutions, banking history and digital payments. SSC and Railway papers touch it in small doses. Almost every answer is a date, a number or a name-and-role pair, so the topic rewards pure revision.

subtopics.title: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
subtopics.concept: The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** is India's central bank. The RBI Act, 1934 created it, and it began work on 1 April 1935. It was nationalised on 1 January 1949. A six-member Monetary Policy Committee now sets the repo rate to keep inflation near 4%.

formulas.note: SDF is the floor of the LAF corridor; banks park surplus cash there without any collateral

formulas.name: MSF ceiling
formulas.note: MSF is the ceiling of the corridor; Bank Rate is kept equal to MSF

tricks.title: Corridor arithmetic
tricks.body: Repo sits in the middle. SDF is repo minus 0.25 (floor). MSF and Bank Rate are repo plus 0.25 (ceiling).

example.q: If the repo rate is 5.25%, what is the SDF rate?
steps: SDF is the floor.
It sits 0.25 below repo.

tricks.title: RBI date anchors
tricks.body: 1926 commission. 1934 Act. 1 April 1935 start. 1937 shift to Mumbai. 1 January 1949 nationalised.

example.q: When did the RBI begin operations?
steps: The Act was passed in 1934.
The bank opened on 1 April 1935.

mistakes: Wrong: Saying the RBI prints the one-rupee note. Right: The Finance Ministry issues the ₹1 note and all coins. The RBI issues every other note.
Wrong: Calling CRR and SLR 'policy rates'. Right: The policy rate is the repo rate. CRR and SLR are reserve ratios.
Wrong: Mixing up 1934 and 1935. Right: 1934 is the Act. 1 April 1935 is when the bank started work.
Wrong: Saying the RBI was nationalised in 1935. Right: It stayed privately held until 1 January 1949.
Wrong: Placing the SDF above the repo rate. Right: SDF is 0.25 below repo (floor). MSF is 0.25 above repo (ceiling).
Wrong: Saying the MPC meets once a year. Right: The Act asks for at least four meetings; in practice there are six.
subtopics.notes:
### What the RBI is
The RBI is the central bank of India. It is the banker to the government and to all banks.

The **Hilton Young Commission (1926)** recommended a central bank. The **RBI Act, 1934** created it. It began work on **1 April 1935**.

Its first head office was in Kolkata. It moved to **Mumbai in 1937**.

Private shareholders owned the RBI at first. The government **nationalised it on 1 January 1949**. So the RBI is now fully owned by the Government of India.

The first Governor was **Sir Osborne Smith**. **C.D. Deshmukh** was the first Indian Governor.

> **Note:** Sanjay Malhotra is the 26th Governor, in charge since December 2024. Office-holders change, so re-check before your exam.

### What the RBI does

| Function | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Monetary authority | Sets interest rates and the money supply |
| Issue of currency | Issues notes, except the ₹1 note and coins |
| Banker to the government | Keeps government accounts, manages its debt |
| Banker's bank | Holds banks' cash reserves, settles their payments |
| Lender of last resort | Lends to banks when no one else will |
| Custodian of forex reserves | Manages the country's foreign exchange reserves |
| Regulator | Licenses and supervises banks |

> **Rule:** The ₹1 note and all coins come from the Finance Ministry. The RBI issues every other note.

### The policy rate corridor

The **repo rate** is the rate at which the RBI lends short-term money to banks against government securities. 'Repo' means repurchase: the bank sells securities and agrees to buy them back.

Repo is the middle of the corridor.

| Rate | Position | Level (Aug 2026) |
|---|---|---|
| MSF = Bank Rate | Repo + 0.25 (ceiling) | 5.50% |
| Repo | Policy rate | 5.25% |
| SDF | Repo - 0.25 (floor) | 5.00% |

The **SDF** (Standing Deposit Facility) takes banks' surplus cash overnight, with no collateral. The **MSF** (Marginal Standing Facility) lends banks overnight cash, even letting them dip into their SLR holdings.

The old **reverse repo** (3.35%) is dormant. Since April 2022 the SDF is the operative floor.

> **Watch:** These levels change. At the August 2026 review, repo was 5.25% and the stance neutral. Verify current figures before your exam.

### CRR and SLR

- **CRR (Cash Reserve Ratio):** the share of deposits a bank keeps as **cash with the RBI**. It earns no interest. It was cut from 4% to 3% in four steps during September-November 2025.
- **SLR (Statutory Liquidity Ratio):** the share a bank keeps **with itself** in liquid assets, such as government securities and gold. It stands at 18%.

> **Tip:** CRR goes to the RBI. SLR stays in the bank's own chest.

Cutting either ratio frees money for lending. Raising them squeezes credit.

### The Monetary Policy Committee

The **RBI (Amendment) Act, 2016** created the MPC, after the Urjit Patel Committee (2014) recommended inflation targeting.

- Six members: the Governor (chair), a Deputy Governor, one RBI officer, and three outside experts named by the government.
- Decisions are by majority. The Governor holds the **casting vote**.
- At least four meetings a year; in practice one every two months.
- Target: **CPI inflation of 4%, with a band of 2% on each side**.
- If inflation stays outside the band for three straight quarters, the RBI must report to the government.

### Other monetary tools

The RBI also uses **OMOs** (buying or selling government securities) and forex swaps. A purchase adds liquidity; a sale drains it.

Day-to-day liquidity runs through the **LAF** (Liquidity Adjustment Facility), using variable-rate repo and reverse repo auctions.

> **Example:** The RBI buys ₹50,000 crore of bonds in an OMO. Cash flows to banks, so liquidity rises.

An OMO sale removes cash; an OMO purchase adds it.

example.q: Which RBI action adds liquidity to the banking system?
steps: Follow the cash.
Buying securities pays cash to banks.

subtopics.title: Banking Structure in India
subtopics.concept: Indian banks come in many shapes: public sector banks, private banks, foreign banks, regional rural banks, cooperative banks and 'differentiated' banks such as payments banks and small finance banks. NBFCs lend money but are not banks. Exams test the special features of each type.

tricks.title: Differentiated banks in one line
tricks.body: Payments banks: take deposits, cannot lend. Small finance banks: full banks that must lend small and to priority sectors.

example.q: Which bank type cannot give loans?
steps: One type is deposit-only.
Payments banks cannot lend.

tricks.title: RRB ownership 50-35-15
tricks.body: Centre 50, sponsor bank 35, state 15. Say it as Centre, sponsor, state.

example.q: What share does the sponsor bank hold in an RRB?
steps: The sponsor sits in the middle of 50-35-15.
The middle share is 35%.

mistakes: Wrong: Calling NBFCs banks. Right: NBFCs lend but cannot accept demand deposits or issue cheques.
Wrong: Saying payments banks can lend after some years. Right: Payments banks can never lend or issue credit cards.
Wrong: Mixing the 1969 and 1980 nationalisation rounds. Right: 1969: 14 banks above ₹50 crore deposits. 1980: 6 banks above ₹200 crore.
Wrong: Giving RRB shares as 40:40:20. Right: RRBs are held 50% by the Centre, 35% by the sponsor bank, 15% by the state.
Wrong: Saying SBI was born in 1806. Right: 1806 is the Bank of Bengal. SBI was formed from the Imperial Bank in 1955.
subtopics.notes:
### How banks are classified
A **scheduled bank** is listed in the **Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934**. It must keep a minimum capital and reserve fund. Scheduled banks enjoy RBI facilities; non-scheduled banks do not.

Commercial banks work for profit. Cooperative banks serve their members. Then come the **differentiated banks**, licensed for a narrow job.

| Type | What it is |
|---|---|
| Public sector bank (PSB) | Government holds the majority stake |
| Private bank | Private shareholders hold the majority |
| Foreign bank | Branch of a bank registered abroad |
| Regional Rural Bank (RRB) | Rural credit, jointly owned by three parties |
| Cooperative bank | Run on cooperative lines |
| Payments bank / Small finance bank | Differentiated banks with narrow mandates |

### Public sector banks

The **Imperial Bank of India** (1921) became the **State Bank of India on 1 July 1955** under the SBI Act, 1955.

**On 19 July 1969**, fourteen big private banks, each with deposits above ₹50 crore, were nationalised. On **15 April 1980**, six more banks with deposits above ₹200 crore joined the list.

In **2017**, the five SBI associate banks and Bharatiya Mahila Bank merged into SBI.

In **April 2020**, ten PSBs merged into four. Punjab National Bank absorbed OBC and United Bank of India. Canara Bank absorbed Syndicate Bank. Union Bank absorbed Andhra Bank and Corporation Bank. Indian Bank absorbed Allahabad Bank.

> **Note:** After the 2020 round, the number of public sector banks stands at **12**.

### Regional Rural Banks

RRBs began on **2 October 1975**. The first one was **Prathama Grameen Bank**. The **RRB Act, 1976** gave them legal form.

An RRB is owned **50% by the Centre, 35% by the sponsor bank and 15% by the state**. It lends to small farmers, artisans and rural workers.

Many mergers have cut the number of RRBs over the years. Check the latest count before your exam.

### Cooperative banks

Cooperative banks work on a 'no profit, no loss' base. Rural ones run in three tiers: the state cooperative bank, the district cooperative bank and the primary society.

Urban cooperative banks (UCBs) face **dual control**: the RBI watches their banking, while the Registrar of Cooperative Societies watches their management.

The **Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2020** strengthened the RBI's grip on UCBs.

### Differentiated banks

The **Nachiket Mor Committee (2014)** proposed payments banks. The RBI licensed both types in 2015.

**Payments banks** take deposits up to **₹2 lakh per customer** (raised from ₹1 lakh in 2021). They cannot lend or issue credit cards. They must invest deposits in government securities. **Airtel Payments Bank** was the first to open (2016-17); **India Post Payments Bank** followed in 2018.

**Small finance banks** can do what any bank does, but must lend **75% of credit to priority sectors** such as farming and small business. **Capital Small Finance Bank** was the first to start (2017).

> **Rule:** Payments banks collect but do not lend. Small finance banks lend but stay small.

### NBFCs and MFIs

A **Non-Banking Financial Company** registers under **Section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934**. It lends and invests like a bank, but:

- it cannot accept **demand deposits**;
- it cannot issue cheques (it sits outside the payment system);
- DICGC deposit insurance does not cover it.

Microfinance institutions (MFIs) give tiny loans to groups, often self-help groups. NABARD's **SHG-Bank Linkage Programme** (1992) connects such groups to banks.

subtopics.title: Banking Terms & Operations
subtopics.concept: Exams love the small words of banking: CASA, NPA, SARFAESI, DICGC and the payment systems NEFT, RTGS, IMPS and UPI. Each carries one definition and one number. Cheque types and the rupee's exchange-rate history complete this block.

tricks.title: Payment-system ladder
tricks.body: RTGS 2004, big and real-time (₹2 lakh minimum). NEFT 2005, batches. IMPS 2010, instant, ₹5 lakh cap. UPI 2016, on the phone, ₹1 lakh usual cap.

example.q: Which system has a minimum of ₹2 lakh?
steps: Only one system has a floor.
RTGS starts at ₹2 lakh.

tricks.title: NPA ladder
tricks.body: 90 days late means NPA. Twelve months more means doubtful. The final stage is loss.

example.q: After how many days is a loan called an NPA?
steps: Interest or instalment stays unpaid.
The cut-off is 90 days.

mistakes: Wrong: Saying DICGC covers the whole deposit. Right: The cover is ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank, principal plus interest together.
Wrong: Mixing RTGS with NEFT. Right: RTGS settles each payment alone and in real time; NEFT settles in batches.
Wrong: Saying SARFAESI works for unsecured loans. Right: SARFAESI needs a secured loan; unsecured loans need the court route.
Wrong: Paying the DICGC premium as a depositor. Right: The bank pays the premium, not the depositor.
Wrong: Treating a post-dated cheque as invalid. Right: A post-dated cheque is valid, but only from its own date.
Wrong: Saying MCLR is older than the base rate. Right: The order is BPLR (2003), base rate (2010), MCLR (2016).
subtopics.notes:
### Accounts, deposits and lending words
**CASA** means Current Account plus Savings Account. These deposits pay little or no interest, so banks call them **low-cost funds**. A high **CASA ratio** lowers a bank's cost of money.

A **demand deposit** is withdrawable any time. A **time deposit** (fixed deposit) runs for a fixed term.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Overdraft | Withdraw more than the balance, within a limit |
| Cash credit | Working-capital loan against stock or assets |
| Demand draft | Prepaid instrument, paid by the bank itself |
| Lien | Bank's right to retain a debtor's asset |

For loans against assets: a **pledge** keeps the goods with the lender. **Hypothecation** leaves the goods with the borrower. A **mortgage** covers immovable property.

### Payment systems: NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, UPI

| System | Year | Speed | Money range |
|---|---|---|---|
| RTGS | 2004 | Real time, one by one | ₹2 lakh minimum, no maximum |
| NEFT | 2005 | Half-hourly batches | No RBI-set minimum |
| IMPS | 2010 | Instant | Up to ₹5 lakh |
| UPI | 2016 | Instant, mobile app | ₹1 lakh usual cap; ₹5 lakh for hospitals, education, capital markets, insurance |

RTGS and NEFT now run **24x7** (December 2020 and December 2019). RTGS means Real Time Gross Settlement: each payment settles alone and in full.

UPI means Unified Payments Interface. It runs on a **virtual payment address (VPA)**, so bank details stay hidden.

> **Tip:** Match the year to the speed: 2004 big, 2005 batch, 2010 instant, 2016 on the phone.

### Bad loans and recovery

A loan becomes an **NPA** (Non-Performing Asset) when interest or instalment stays unpaid for **90 days**. Then it moves: sub-standard (an NPA for 12 months), doubtful, and finally loss.

- **SARFAESI Act, 2002:** a secured creditor bank can seize and sell pledged property **without going to court**. It does not cover unsecured loans or agricultural land.
- **Debts Recovery Tribunals** (RDDBFI Act, 1993) hear bank recovery cases.
- The **Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016** is the modern route for dead companies, run through the NCLT.

> **Rule:** SARFAESI needs security. No security means no seizure without court help.

### Deposit insurance: DICGC

The **Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation** was formed in **1978** by merging the Deposit Insurance Corporation (1962) with a credit guarantee body.

- It insures **₹5 lakh per depositor per bank** (raised from ₹1 lakh in 2020), counting principal and interest together.
- It covers licensed banks: commercial banks, RRBs, cooperative banks and small finance banks. NBFCs sit outside.
- The **bank pays the premium**, not the depositor.

> **Example:** You keep ₹6 lakh in one bank. If it fails, DICGC pays ₹5 lakh; the rest follows liquidation.

### Cheques and instruments

A **bearer cheque** pays whoever holds it. An **order cheque** pays the named person. A **crossed cheque** must go through a bank account.

- A cheque is valid for **3 months** from its date (the rule since 2012).
- **Post-dated:** dated ahead; valid from that date. **Stale:** older than three months. **Self:** 'self' means the drawer's own account.

> **Watch:** Exams swap bearer and order, or pay a crossed cheque at the counter.

### Loan pricing and the rupee

Loan pricing moved in steps: **BPLR (2003) to base rate (2010) to MCLR (2016) to repo-linked EBLR (2019)**. MCLR is the Marginal Cost of funds based Lending Rate.

The rupee's external value was officially fixed (the par value system) till 1991. It was **devalued twice in July 1991**. **LERMS (March 1992)** ran a dual rate: 40% of foreign exchange at the official rate, 60% at the market rate. The rates were **unified in March 1993**.

It skips unsecured loans and agricultural land.

patterns.name: Cheque types and validity
patterns.howToSpot: The question says 'a crossed cheque is payable', 'a cheque is valid for', or swaps bearer with order.
steps: Bearer pays the holder; order pays the named person.
Crossed cheques must go through a bank account.
Validity: 3 months from the date of issue.
patterns.why: Each word on the cheque points to one payer.

example.q: A crossed cheque must be paid how?
steps: Two parallel lines cross its face.
Cash over the counter is barred.
example.answer: Only by credit to a bank account

patterns.name: Banking jargon and exchange-rate history
patterns.howToSpot: The question expands CASA, matches lien, pledge, hypothecation and mortgage, or asks about LERMS and the 1991 devaluation.
steps: CASA = current account + savings account, the cheapest funds.
Pledge: goods with lender. Hypothecation: goods with borrower. Mortgage: immovable property.
Par value till 1991, devaluation July 1991, LERMS March 1992, unified March 1993.
patterns.why: These are one-line recall items.

example.q: The LERMS of 1992 was a system of what?
steps: It came after the 1991 devaluation.
It split foreign exchange conversions in two.
example.answer: A dual exchange rate (40% official, 60% market)

RTGS 2004 (min ₹2 lakh), NEFT 2005 (batches), IMPS 2010 (₹5 lakh), UPI 2016 (₹1 lakh usual).
Both RTGS and NEFT run 24x7 (Dec 2020 and Dec 2019).
NPA at 90 days: sub-standard, then doubtful after 12 months, then loss.
SARFAESI 2002: seize secured assets without court; DRT 1993; IBC 2016.
DICGC: ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank; the bank pays the premium.

subtopics.title: Financial Institutions & Regulators
subtopics.concept: Beside the RBI stand big specialised bodies: NABARD for farming, SIDBI for small industry, EXIM for exports, NHB for housing, and the regulators SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA. Exams pair each body with a year, a headquarters and a role.

tricks.title: Year ladder
tricks.body: NABARD 1982, EXIM 1982, NHB 1988, SIDBI 1990, SEBI Act 1992, IRDAI 1999, PFRDA Act 2013.

example.q: Which body came first, NABARD or SIDBI?
steps: The refinance bodies came before the new regulators.
NABARD is 1982; SIDBI is 1990.

tricks.title: Headquarters pairs

subtopics.notes:
### The refinance family
These bodies do not take deposits from the public. They **refinance** — they lend to banks and lenders that lend onward.

| Institution | Set up | HQ | Job |
|---|---|---|---|
| NABARD | 12 July 1982 | Mumbai | Apex bank for farm and rural credit |
| EXIM Bank | 1982 | Mumbai | Finance exports and imports |
| NHB | 9 July 1988 | New Delhi | Housing finance regulator and refinance |
| SIDBI | 2 April 1990 | Lucknow | Apex bank for MSMEs |

**NABARD** came on the **Sivaraman Committee's** advice. It took over the RBI's agricultural credit role and absorbed the **ARDC** (Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation). It also runs the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme for women's groups.

**SIDBI** was created under the **SIDBI Act, 1989** and began work on **2 April 1990**. It is the apex body for small industries and runs **MUDRA** (2015) as its subsidiary.

**EXIM Bank** works under the **EXIM Bank Act, 1981**. It began operations in 1982. It gives export credit, extends lines of credit to foreign governments and supports Indian project exporters abroad.

**NHB** works under the **NHB Act, 1987**. The RBI held its entire share until 2019, when ownership passed to the government. NHB refinances housing finance companies and keeps watch over the housing finance sector.

> **Tip:** NABARD = fields. SIDBI = workshops. EXIM = ports. NHB = homes.

### Market regulators

| Regulator | Statutory from | HQ | Regulates |
|---|---|---|---|
| SEBI | 1992 (set up 1988) | Mumbai | Securities markets |
| IRDAI | 1999 (IRDA Act) | Hyderabad | Insurance |
| PFRDA | 2013 (set up 2003) | New Delhi | Pension funds |

**SEBI** began as a non-statutory body in **April 1988**. The **SEBI Act, 1992** gave it legal teeth after the securities scam.

The **IRDA Act, 1999** opened insurance to private players and set up the **IRDAI**, ending LIC's monopoly.

**PFRDA** worked from **2003** and became statutory through the **PFRDA Act, 2013**.

> **Rule:** Set-up year and statutory year differ for SEBI and PFRDA. When the question says 'statutory', give the Act year.

### Pensions

The **National Pension System (NPS)** began for government employees in **2004** and opened to all citizens in **2009**. **Atal Pension Yojana (2015)** covers unorganised workers. PFRDA oversees both.

### Coordinating bodies

The **Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC)**, set up in **2010**, is chaired by the **Union Finance Minister**. It coordinates regulators such as the RBI, SEBI and IRDAI.

> **Example:** A bank wants refinance for farm loans: it goes to NABARD. For a housing loan portfolio: NHB. For a small-firm loan pool: SIDBI. For export credit: EXIM Bank.

subtopics.title: Banking History & Reforms
subtopics.concept: Indian banking grew from trading houses in the 1700s to today's 12 public sector banks. The turning points are the 1969-80 nationalisation, the 1991 liberalisation with the Narasimham Committees, and the mergers of 2017-2020.

tricks.title: Timeline story

tricks.title: Committee anchors

mistakes: Wrong: Calling 1998 the year of the first Narasimham report. Right: Report I is 1991; report II is 1998.
Wrong: Saying Basel I dealt with market risk. Right: Basel I (1988) set credit-risk capital; Basel II added the three pillars.
Wrong: Mixing the SBI year (1955) with the Imperial Bank year (1921). Right: The Imperial Bank was formed in 1921; SBI in 1955.
Wrong: Saying India's capital adequacy norm is 8%. Right: Basel sets 8%; the RBI keeps it higher, at 9%.
Wrong: Placing the PSB mega-merger in 2017. Right: 2017 was the SBI associates merger; the 10-into-4 merger ran from 2019 to 2020.
subtopics.notes:
### The early banks
The **Bank of Hindostan (1770)** was the first bank in India. It later failed.

Three **presidency banks** came next: Bank of Bengal (1806), Bank of Bombay (1840) and Bank of Madras (1843). They merged in **1921** to form the **Imperial Bank of India**.

**Allahabad Bank (1865)** is the oldest surviving joint-stock bank. **Punjab National Bank (1894)** was the first bank fully managed by Indians. The **Central Bank of India (1911)** was the first wholly owned and managed by Indians.

> **Note:** The Swadeshi movement of the early 1900s bred many of these banks.

### The nationalisation era

| Year | Event |
|---|---|
| 1949 | RBI nationalised; the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 gave RBI supervisory powers |
| 1955 | SBI created from the Imperial Bank |
| 1969 | 14 banks nationalised on 19 July |
| 1975 | Regional Rural Banks started |
| 1980 | 6 more banks nationalised on 15 April |

The government nationalised banks to push credit to farming, small industry and the poor. The **Lead Bank Scheme (1969)** assigned each district to one bank.

> **Rule:** 1969 means 14 banks and ₹50 crore. 1980 means 6 banks and ₹200 crore.

### Liberalisation of 1991 and Narasimham

A balance-of-payments crisis forced the reforms of **1991**: the rupee was devalued, controls were loosened, and new private banks were licensed.

The **Narasimham Committee I (1991)** asked for lower reserve requirements, prudential norms for bad loans, and free entry for private banks. The **Narasimham Committee II (1998)** urged mergers to build a few strong banks and a lower government stake.

> **Tip:** One in 1991 opens the door. Two in 1998 builds stronger banks.

### Basel norms in brief

| Norm | Year | Main idea |
|---|---|---|
| Basel I | 1988 | Minimum capital for credit risk (8%) |
| Basel II | 2004 | Three pillars: capital, supervision, market discipline |
| Basel III | 2010 | More and better capital, plus liquidity buffers |

India implemented Basel III from **1 April 2013**. The RBI keeps the minimum total capital ratio at **9%**, above Basel's 8%.

> **Example:** Basel III was born after the 2008 global crisis, which showed how fast bank funding can dry up.

### Consolidation after 2017

In **2017**, the five associate banks of SBI and Bharatiya Mahila Bank merged into SBI.

Announced in **August 2019** and effective **1 April 2020**, the mega-merger folded ten PSBs into four. Punjab National Bank took in OBC and United Bank of India. Canara Bank took in Syndicate Bank. Union Bank took in Andhra Bank and Corporation Bank. Indian Bank took in Allahabad Bank.

The count fell to **12 public sector banks**.

> **Watch:** RRBs have also been merged in several rounds. Check the current count before your exam.

subtopics.concept: India's retail payments run through NPCI, set up in 2008: RuPay cards, IMPS, UPI and more. The RBI's digital rupee is legal tender in digital form. Inclusion schemes such as PMJDY, MUDRA and the Kisan Credit Card carry banking to every household.

subtopics.notes:
### NPCI and its products
The **National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI)** was set up in **2008** under the RBI and the banking industry. It runs most retail payment rails.

| Product | Year | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| AePS | 2010 | Bank services at a MicroATM using Aadhaar and a fingerprint |
| RuPay | 2012 | India's own card network |
| UPI | 2016 | Instant payments from a phone |
| Bharat BillPay | 2016 | One network for utility bills |
| BHIM | Dec 2016 | The government's UPI app |
| NETC FASTag | 2016 | Toll payment stickers |

> **Tip:** AePS is the rural door: no phone needed, just Aadhaar and a fingerprint at a banking correspondent's machine.

### UPI in detail

UPI (Unified Payments Interface) went live in **April 2016**. Payments use a **virtual payment address (VPA)**, so bank details stay private.

- Usual cap: **₹1 lakh per transaction**. Hospitals, education, capital markets and insurance carry **₹5 lakh** limits.
- **UPI AutoPay** (2020) handles recurring payments. **UPI Lite** (2022) makes small payments without touching the core banking system. **UPI 123PAY** (2022) works on button phones.
- In **February 2023** UPI linked with Singapore's PayNow, the first cross-country link.

### The digital rupee

The RBI's **Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC)** is called the **digital rupee (e₹)**. It is legal tender, like notes, but exists digitally. Wholesale pilots began on **1 November 2022** and retail pilots on **1 December 2022**.

> **Rule:** Cryptocurrencies are private and unregulated. The digital rupee is the RBI's own money.

### Financial inclusion schemes

| Scheme | Year | Key feature |
|---|---|---|
| PMJDY | 2014 | Zero-balance account, RuPay card, ₹2 lakh accident cover, ₹10,000 overdraft |
| Kisan Credit Card | 1998 | Cheap crop loans to farmers |
| MUDRA (PMMY) | 2015 | Collateral-free small business loans |
| Atal Pension Yojana | 2015 | Assured pension for unorganised workers |

MUDRA loans come in slabs: **Shishu** up to ₹50,000, **Kishore** ₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh, **Tarun** ₹5 lakh to ₹10 lakh. A **Tarun Plus** slab (up to ₹20 lakh) was added in 2024 for borrowers who repaid a Tarun loan.

Priority sector rules push banks to lend to farming, small firms and weaker sections: **40% of bank credit** for universal banks.

> **Watch:** PMJDY is 28 August 2014; MUDRA is 8 April 2015. Exams swap these two years often.

### Banking access and customer care

**White-label ATMs**, allowed from 2013, are owned by non-bank companies. **India Post Payments Bank (2018)** carries banking to the post office.

For complaints, the **RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (2021)** replaced the old Banking Ombudsman Scheme of 1995. One ombudsman now covers all complaints, filed free on the RBI's central portal.

> **Example:** A customer's UPI payment fails and the bank does not help. After 30 days, the RBI's ombudsman portal is the next stop.

Accepting deposits from the general public and giving retail loans
Acting as lender of last resort to commercial banks
solvedExamples.solution: The RBI is the **bankers' bank** — it keeps banks' reserves and lends to them as the lender of last resort. **Accepting deposits from the public is the job of commercial banks**, not of the central bank. The RBI issues all notes except the ₹1 note, which comes from the Finance Ministry.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Public deposits = commercial banks. The RBI banks the banks.

solvedExamples.q:
Consider the following statements about payments banks in India:
1. They can accept deposits up to ₹2 lakh per customer.
2. They can issue credit cards to their customers.
3. They cannot undertake lending activities.

Which of the statements are correct?
solvedExamples.solution: Payments banks take deposits up to **₹2 lakh per customer** and **cannot lend or issue credit cards** — so statements 1 and 3 are correct and 2 is wrong. They invest deposits in government securities; the model came from the Nachiket Mor Committee (2014).
solvedExamples.pattern: payments banks vs small finance banks

solvedExamples.q: In its August 2026 monetary policy review, the RBI kept the repo rate unchanged at 5.25%. Under the liquidity framework, the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) rate at that time was:
solvedExamples.solution: Repo is the middle of the corridor. **MSF = Bank Rate = repo + 0.25% = 5.50%**, and the SDF floor = repo - 0.25% = 5.00%. Positions stay fixed even when levels change, so learn the plus-minus 0.25 rule rather than the numbers themselves (and re-check the current rate before your exam).

solvedExamples.q: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
solvedExamples.solution: **NABARD — 1982** is correct (set up on 12 July 1982 on the Sivaraman Committee's advice). SIDBI came in 1990, EXIM Bank in 1982 and NHB in 1988.

practice.q: The Reserve Bank of India was established under which Act?
options: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1935
practice.solution: The **RBI Act, 1934** created the Reserve Bank on the Hilton Young Commission's recommendation; it began work on 1 April 1935. The Banking Regulation Act came later, in 1949.
practice.shortcut: Act first, bank next: 1934 Act, 1 April 1935 opening.

practice.q: The one-rupee note in India is issued by:
options: The Ministry of Finance, Government of India
practice.solution: The RBI issues all notes **except the ₹1 note**. The Finance Ministry issues the ₹1 note and all coins; the note is signed by the Finance Secretary.

practice.q: In the RBI's liquidity corridor, the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) rate is always kept:
practice.solution: Repo sits in the middle: **MSF = Bank Rate = repo + 0.25%** (ceiling) and **SDF = repo - 0.25%** (floor).
practice.shortcut: Floor minus 0.25, ceiling plus 0.25 — MSF is the ceiling.

practice.q: How many members constitute the Monetary Policy Committee of the RBI?
practice.solution: The MPC has **six members** — three from the RBI (including the Governor as chair) and three appointed by the government. The Governor holds the casting vote.

practice.q: Under the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), a bank must keep:
options: Cash with the RBI, which earns no interest
Cash in its own vault only
practice.solution: CRR is a share of deposits kept as **cash with the RBI**, and it **earns no interest**. Liquid assets kept **with the bank itself** form the SLR.
practice.shortcut: CRR = Cash to RBI; SLR = Securities at Self.

practice.q: Which of the following RBI actions will reduce liquidity in the banking system?
options: Buying government securities in an open market operation
practice.solution: A **CRR rise** locks more cash with the RBI, leaving banks less to lend. Repo cuts, OMO purchases and SLR cuts all release money.
practice.shortcut: Follow the cash: RBI takes money in, so liquidity falls.

practice.q: Who was the first Indian Governor of the Reserve Bank of India?
practice.solution: **Sir C.D. Deshmukh** became the first Indian Governor in 1943. Sir Osborne Smith (1935) was the first Governor of any nationality; Sir James Braid Taylor was the second.

practice.q: The ₹1 currency note in India is signed by:
options: The Deputy Governor of the RBI
practice.solution: Since the Finance Ministry issues the ₹1 note, it carries the signature of the **Finance Secretary**. All other notes are signed by the RBI Governor.
practice.shortcut: ₹1 note: a government issuer, so a government signature.

practice.q: If the RBI repo rate is 5.25% (as at its August 2026 review), the operative floor of the liquidity corridor is:
practice.solution: Since April 2022 the corridor floor is the **SDF = repo - 0.25% = 5.00%**. The dormant reverse repo (3.35%) is no longer the floor; the MSF/Bank Rate ceiling would be 5.50%. Levels change with policy, so always re-check the latest review.

practice.q: Under the flexible inflation targeting framework, if average CPI inflation stays outside the 2-6% band for three consecutive quarters, the RBI must:
options: Report to the Central Government stating the reasons and remedies
practice.solution: The failure clause requires the RBI to **report to the government in writing** — why the target failed, what it will do, and the time needed to return to target.

practice.q: Which of the following can a bank count as Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) assets?
options: Cash, gold and approved government securities held with itself
practice.solution: SLR assets are **cash, gold and unencumbered approved securities (mainly government securities) held by the bank itself**. Corporate bonds and loans do not qualify.

practice.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. The Bank Rate is kept equal to the MSF rate.
2. The dormant reverse repo rate of 3.35% is currently the operative floor of the liquidity corridor.
3. The SDF allows banks to park funds with the RBI without providing collateral.

Which of the statements are correct?
practice.solution: Statement 1 is correct — the Bank Rate moves with the MSF. Statement 3 is correct — the SDF needs no collateral. Statement 2 is wrong: since **April 2022 the SDF, not the dormant reverse repo (3.35%), is the operative floor**.
practice.shortcut: Reverse repo is dormant; the SDF is the working floor.

practice.q: A scheduled bank in India is one which is included in:
options: The First Schedule of the Constitution
The Second Schedule of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
The Seventh Schedule of the Constitution
practice.solution: Scheduled banks are listed in the **Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934**. They must carry a minimum paid-up capital and reserves, and they enjoy RBI facilities such as refinance and clearing membership.

practice.q: How many commercial banks were nationalised on 19 July 1969?
practice.solution: **Fourteen** banks, each with deposits above ₹50 crore, were nationalised on 19 July 1969. Six more followed on 15 April 1980.

practice.q: Which of the following activities can a payments bank undertake?
options: Accepting demand deposits up to ₹2 lakh per customer
Accepting deposits of any amount from corporates
practice.solution: Payments banks may **accept deposits up to ₹2 lakh per customer**, but they **cannot lend or issue credit cards**. They invest deposits in government securities.
practice.shortcut: Payments bank = a deposit box with no loan desk.

practice.q: In a Regional Rural Bank, the shareholding pattern is:
practice.solution: RRBs are owned **50% by the Central Government, 35% by the sponsor bank and 15% by the State Government**.

practice.q: Which of the following is NOT true about Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs)?
options: They are registered under Section 45-IA of the RBI Act, 1934
They can lend and make investments
They can issue cheques to their customers
DICGC insurance does not cover their deposits
practice.solution: NBFCs **cannot issue cheques** because they lie outside the payment and settlement system. The other statements are true: registration under Section 45-IA, lending rights, and no DICGC cover.
practice.shortcut: The NBFC's three 'noes': no demand deposits, no cheques, no DICGC.

practice.q: The State Bank of India was created in 1955 by nationalising:
practice.solution: The **Imperial Bank of India** (1921), built from the three presidency banks, became the **State Bank of India on 1 July 1955**.
practice.shortcut: Presidency banks, Imperial Bank (1921), then SBI (1955).

practice.q: Which of the following facilities is available to scheduled banks?
options: Membership of the RBI clearing house and RBI refinance facilities
practice.solution: Scheduled banks gain **clearing-house membership, RBI refinance and short-term borrowing facilities**. All banks — scheduled or not — remain subject to reserve requirements, inspection and the ban on note issue.

practice.q: The second round of bank nationalisation (15 April 1980) covered banks with deposits of at least:
practice.solution: The **1980 round** took in **six banks with deposits of ₹200 crore or more**. The 1969 round used the ₹50 crore threshold for its fourteen banks.
practice.shortcut: 14 with ₹50 crore in 1969; 6 with ₹200 crore in 1980.

practice.q: A small finance bank must extend what share of its credit to priority sectors such as agriculture and small business?
practice.solution: Small finance banks must lend **75% of their adjusted net bank credit to priority sectors**. Universal banks carry a 40% priority-sector target.

practice.q: The first Regional Rural Bank, set up on 2 October 1975, was:
practice.solution: **Prathama Grameen Bank** opened on 2 October 1975 and became the model for the RRB network formalised by the RRB Act, 1976.

practice.q: Under which provision of the RBI Act, 1934 are Non-Banking Financial Companies registered?
practice.solution: **Section 45-IA** of the RBI Act, 1934 requires NBFCs to register with the RBI. Section 22 covers bank licences; Section 35A covers RBI directions to banks.

practice.q: With effect from 1 April 2020, Syndicate Bank was merged with:
practice.solution: In the 2019-20 consolidation, **Canara Bank absorbed Syndicate Bank**. PNB took in OBC and United Bank of India; Union Bank took in Andhra Bank and Corporation Bank; Indian Bank took in Allahabad Bank — leaving 12 PSBs.
practice.shortcut: Two Karnataka giants: Canara and Syndicate.

practice.q: The minimum amount that can be transferred through RTGS is:
practice.solution: **RTGS carries a minimum of ₹2 lakh** with no upper limit set by the RBI. It settles each transaction individually and in real time.

practice.q: A loan becomes a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) when interest or instalment remains overdue for more than:
practice.solution: The NPA trigger is **90 days** of overdue interest or instalment. After 12 months as an NPA it becomes doubtful.

practice.q: Under the SARFAESI Act, 2002, a secured creditor bank can:
options: Seize and sell secured assets without approaching the court
Recover unsecured loans directly from salaries
Declare the borrower bankrupt in a civil court
practice.solution: **SARFAESI lets banks enforce security — seize and sell pledged or mortgaged assets — without court intervention**. Unsecured loans and agricultural land fall outside the Act.

practice.q: The DICGC insures bank deposits up to:
practice.solution: The cover is **₹5 lakh per depositor per bank**, counting principal and interest together. It was raised from ₹1 lakh in 2020.

practice.q: A crossed cheque is one which:
options: Is payable to the bearer over the counter
Can be collected only through a bank account
Is always payable after three months
practice.solution: Two parallel lines 'cross' the cheque and bar cash over the counter; the amount must go **into a bank account**. Crossing has nothing to do with validity periods.

practice.q: In banking, CASA stands for:
options: Central Account for Savings and Assets
practice.solution: **CASA = Current Account + Savings Account**. These deposits cost the bank almost nothing, so a high CASA ratio means cheaper funds.

practice.q: NEFT has been available round the clock (24x7) since:
practice.solution: **NEFT went 24x7 in December 2019**; RTGS followed in December 2020.
practice.shortcut: N before R: NEFT first (2019), RTGS later (2020).

practice.q: An asset that has remained sub-standard for a period of 12 months is classified as:
practice.solution: An NPA that stays sub-standard for **12 months** moves to the **doubtful** category. A loss asset is one identified as a loss with little hope of recovery.

practice.q: Which of the following is outside the scope of the SARFAESI Act, 2002?
options: A mortgage on a factory building
Pledge of goods with a bank
A loan secured by agricultural land
practice.solution: The Act excludes **agricultural land** (along with unsecured loans). Factory mortgages, pledged goods and hypothecated vehicles can all be enforced under SARFAESI.

practice.q: Which statement about DICGC deposit insurance is correct?
options: The depositor pays the premium to DICGC
All deposits of one depositor in one bank are counted together for the ₹5 lakh limit
practice.solution: DICGC adds up **all deposits of one depositor in one bank** — savings plus fixed — for the ₹5 lakh cap. The bank pays the premium; NBFC deposits are not covered; coverage extends to all licensed banks.
practice.shortcut: Count per person per bank, not per account.

practice.q: Since 1 April 2012, cheques, demand drafts and pay orders in India are valid for:
practice.solution: The validity period is **three months** from the date of the instrument; older instruments are treated as stale.

practice.q: The Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System (LERMS), introduced in March 1992, was a system of:
options: A fixed exchange rate pegged to gold
A dual exchange rate with 40% of transactions at the official rate and 60% at the market rate
practice.solution: **LERMS ran a dual rate: 40% of foreign exchange was converted at the official rate and 60% at the market rate.** The rates were unified into a single market-determined rate in March 1993.

practice.q: NABARD was established in:
practice.solution: **NABARD** (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) was set up on **12 July 1982** on the Sivaraman Committee's recommendation, with headquarters in Mumbai.

practice.q: The headquarters of the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) is at:
practice.solution: IRDAI sits in **Hyderabad**. Mumbai holds SEBI and NABARD; Delhi holds NHB and PFRDA.

practice.q: Which institution is the apex body for financing India's foreign trade?
practice.solution: The **Export-Import Bank of India (EXIM Bank)**, set up in 1982 under the EXIM Bank Act, 1981, is the apex institution for export credit.

practice.q: NABARD was set up on the recommendations of which committee?
practice.solution: The **Sivaraman Committee** (1981) proposed a national bank for farm and rural credit, which took shape as NABARD in 1982.

practice.q: SEBI became a statutory body through the SEBI Act of:
practice.solution: SEBI was formed in **April 1988** as a non-statutory body and received legal powers from the **SEBI Act, 1992**, passed after the securities scam.

practice.q: SIDBI was established on 2 April:
practice.solution: The Small Industries Development Bank of India began on **2 April 1990** under the SIDBI Act, 1989, with headquarters in Lucknow.

practice.q: The headquarters of SIDBI is located at:
practice.solution: **Lucknow** houses SIDBI. NABARD and EXIM sit in Mumbai.

practice.q: Which institution is the apex refinancing body for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and also runs the MUDRA Yojana?
practice.solution: **SIDBI** refinances MSME credit and administers MUDRA (2015), which refinances small business loans, as its subsidiary.

practice.q: While setting up NABARD in 1982, which of the following was merged with it?
options: The Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation (ARDC)
practice.solution: NABARD took over the **ARDC**, along with the RBI's agricultural credit functions.

practice.q: PFRDA became a statutory regulator through:
practice.solution: PFRDA worked from **2003** on an executive footing; the **PFRDA Act, 2013** made it statutory.

practice.q: The IRDA Act, 1999 is remembered mainly because it:
options: Ended the monopoly of LIC and opened insurance to private players
practice.solution: The **IRDA Act, 1999** ended LIC's monopoly and let private insurers in, while creating IRDAI as the regulator. The 74% FDI limit came from a 2021 amendment.

practice.q:
Consider the following statements:
1. NHB was set up in 1988 and was wholly owned by the RBI until 2019.
2. The Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) is chaired by the Union Finance Minister.
3. NABARD's headquarters is in New Delhi.

Which of the statements are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are correct — NHB passed wholly to the government in 2019, and FSDC (2010) is chaired by the Finance Minister. Statement 3 is wrong: **NABARD's headquarters is Mumbai**.

practice.q: The first bank established in India was:
practice.solution: The **Bank of Hindostan (1770)**, set up by a European agency house in Calcutta, was the first bank in India. It later failed.

practice.q: The State Bank of India was formed in which year?
practice.solution: **1955** — the Imperial Bank of India became the State Bank of India under the SBI Act, 1955. 1921 was the Imperial Bank's own birth year.

practice.q: The first Narasimham Committee on the financial system submitted its report in:
practice.solution: **Narasimham I reported in 1991**, alongside the liberalisation reforms; Narasimham II followed in 1998.

practice.q: The 'three pillars' — minimum capital requirements, supervisory review process and market discipline — belong to:
practice.solution: **Basel II (2004)** built the three pillars. Basel I (1988) set the first credit-risk capital floor; Basel III (2010) added richer capital and liquidity rules.

practice.q: With effect from 1 April 2020, United Bank of India and Oriental Bank of Commerce were merged into:
practice.solution: **PNB absorbed OBC and United Bank of India** in the 2020 round, which cut the PSB count to 12.
practice.shortcut: The two Bengal-side banks joined PNB.

practice.q: Which of the following is the correct chronological order of events?
options: RBI nationalised, SBI formed, Imperial Bank formed, RRBs started
Imperial Bank formed, RBI nationalised, SBI formed, RRBs started
SBI formed, Imperial Bank formed, RBI nationalised, RRBs started
Imperial Bank formed, SBI formed, RBI nationalised, RRBs started
practice.solution: The sequence is: Imperial Bank (1921), RBI nationalised (1949), SBI (1955), RRBs (1975).

practice.q: Which bank was the first commercial bank wholly owned and managed by Indians?
practice.solution: The **Central Bank of India (1911)** was the first bank wholly owned and managed by Indians. PNB (1894) was the first fully Indian-managed bank.

practice.q: The fourteen banks nationalised in 1969 were those with deposits above:
practice.solution: The **₹50 crore** deposit cut-off selected the fourteen banks of 19 July 1969. Six more banks above ₹200 crore followed in 1980.

practice.q: The second Narasimham Committee (1998) is chiefly associated with which recommendation?
options: Merging strong banks and reducing government stakes in banks
practice.solution: **Narasimham II (1998)** urged mergers into a few strong banks and a lower government holding. The Lead Bank Scheme is 1969; GST came in 2017.

practice.q: Which of the following statements about Basel norms in India is correct?
options: India adopted Basel III norms from 1 April 2013 with a minimum total capital of 9%
Basel I norms dealt with market risk only
India follows the Basel minimum of 8% exactly
Basel III was announced before the 2008 financial crisis
practice.solution: India implemented **Basel III from 1 April 2013** and keeps the minimum total capital at **9%**, above Basel's 8%. Basel I (1988) dealt with credit risk; Basel III followed the 2008 crisis.

practice.q: Allahabad Bank, set up in 1865, was merged (in 2020) into which bank?
practice.solution: The 2019-20 round folded **Allahabad Bank into Indian Bank**. Allahabad Bank itself is the oldest surviving joint-stock bank in India (1865).

practice.q:
Arrange the following in chronological order:
1. Enactment of the Banking Regulation Act
2. Nationalisation of 14 banks
3. Foundation of the Imperial Bank of India
4. Start of Regional Rural Banks

Which order is correct?
practice.solution: Imperial Bank (1921), Banking Regulation Act (1949), 14 banks nationalised (1969), RRBs (1975).

practice.q: The Unified Payments Interface (UPI) was launched in:
practice.solution: **UPI went live in April 2016**, built by NPCI. BHIM, the government's UPI app, followed in December 2016.

practice.q: In UPI, a virtual payment address (VPA) is used to:
options: Fix the interest rate on payments
Identify the user without revealing bank account details
Charge a fee on each payment
practice.solution: A VPA (like name@bank) routes payments **without exposing account numbers or IFSC codes**.

practice.q: The digital rupee (e₹), whose pilots began in 2022, is best described as:
options: A private cryptocurrency regulated by SEBI
Legal tender issued by the Reserve Bank of India in digital form
A prepaid wallet issued by banks
A new series of polymer notes
practice.solution: The e₹ is the RBI's **central bank digital currency — sovereign legal tender in digital form**. Wholesale pilots began on 1 November 2022 and retail pilots on 1 December 2022.
practice.shortcut: CBDC = the central bank's own digital cash.

practice.q: The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) was launched on:
practice.solution: **28 August 2014** marks PMJDY's launch. 8 April 2015 belongs to MUDRA; 15 August 2014 was only the announcement day.

practice.q: A collateral-free MUDRA loan of ₹3 lakh falls under which category?
practice.solution: **Kishore covers ₹50,000 to ₹5 lakh**. Shishu runs up to ₹50,000, Tarun ₹5-10 lakh, and Tarun Plus up to ₹20 lakh for past Tarun borrowers.
practice.shortcut: Shishu tiny, Kishore mid, Tarun big.

practice.q: A white-label ATM is one which:
options: Is owned and operated by a non-bank company
Belongs exclusively to the State Bank of India
practice.solution: White-label ATMs are **owned by non-bank companies**, first allowed in 2013. In brown-label ATMs, the bank only provides the branding.

practice.q: RuPay, India's own card payment network, was launched by NPCI in:
practice.solution: **RuPay launched in 2012** as the domestic alternative to international card networks.

practice.q: For which of the following payment categories has a higher UPI per-transaction limit of ₹5 lakh (against the usual ₹1 lakh) been provided?
options: Payments to hospitals and educational institutions
practice.solution: **Hospitals, educational institutions, capital markets and insurance** carry ₹5 lakh per-transaction limits; the usual UPI cap is ₹1 lakh.
practice.shortcut: Big bills (health, education, markets, insurance) = ₹5 lakh.

practice.q: Which of the following statements about India's digital payment systems is correct?
options: The retail pilot of the digital rupee began on 1 December 2022
AePS requires a smartphone and internet
UPI payments cannot be made to merchants
practice.solution: The **retail e₹ pilot began on 1 December 2022** (wholesale: 1 November 2022). BHIM came after UPI; AePS works on MicroATMs with a fingerprint, no smartphone needed; UPI serves merchants fully.

practice.q: Under PMJDY, the overdraft facility offered in basic accounts is up to:
practice.solution: PMJDY accounts carry a **₹10,000 overdraft** facility, a RuPay debit card with ₹2 lakh accident cover, and no minimum balance requirement.

practice.q: The 'Tarun Plus' category under the PM MUDRA scheme, introduced in 2024, offers loans up to:
practice.solution: **Tarun Plus gives up to ₹20 lakh** to entrepreneurs who have repaid a previous Tarun loan. It is the fourth MUDRA slab, after Shishu, Kishore and Tarun.

practice.q: The RBI's single, integrated scheme for resolving customer complaints against banks and other regulated entities was introduced in:
practice.solution: The **RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021** merged the old Banking Ombudsman Scheme (1995) and other schemes into one cost-free complaint route through the RBI's central portal.
